title: Assets across pension types
gist: US private defined contribution pension assets rose from $9.20T (2021 Q4) to $12.27T (2026 Q2) while defined benefit assets fell from $3.68T to $3.07T; the FRED Blog attributes the widening gap to equity-heavy DC vs bond-heavy DB allocations rather than enrollment. The flip side is volatility: DC assets fell 30% in the Great Recession while DB assets rose 5%.

themes.theme: DC vs DB asset divergence since 2021

insights.claim: US private-sector defined contribution (DC) pension assets grew from $9.20 trillion in 2021 Q4 to $12.27 trillion in 2026 Q2 (~+33%).
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Household retirement wealth is increasingly concentrated in self-directed, equity-heavy accounts, amplifying wealth effects from stock market moves.
insights.quote: DC assets grew from $9.20 trillion to $12.27 trillion

insights.claim: US private-sector defined benefit (DB) pension assets fell from $3.68 trillion in 2021 Q4 to $3.07 trillion in 2026 Q2 (~-17%), even as DC assets rose.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Bond-heavy DB portfolios were hit by the post-2021 rate rise; DB plans are a shrinking slice of the pension asset pool.
insights.quote: DB assets fell from $3.68 trillion to $3.07 trillion over the same period

insights.claim: The gap in asset value between private DC and DB pensions has widened increasingly since late 2021, with DC now roughly 4x DB assets.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Retirement-system risk is shifting from employers' balance sheets to households.
insights.quote: the gap in asset value between the two pension types has grown increasingly wide since late 2021

insights.claim: Enrollment in DC pensions is about four times that of DB pensions, but that enrollment gap has been stable since 2013, so it likely does not explain the recent widening in asset values.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The divergence is a returns/asset-allocation story, not a demographic or participation shift.
insights.quote: while enrollment in DC pensions is four times greater than enrollment in DB pensions, the enrollment gap has held steady since 2013

insights.claim: The greater value of DC pension assets is probably attributable to different investment allocations between the two pension types rather than enrollment differences.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Relative performance of equities vs bonds should drive the DC/DB asset ratio going forward.
insights.quote: the greater value of DC pension assets can probably be attributed to the different investment distributions between the pension types

insights.claim: DC account holders seek to maximize retirement income and thus tilt toward riskier, higher-return assets like stocks, while DB sponsors prioritize meeting fixed obligations and favor safer, lower-return assets like bonds.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Structural growth of DC plans implies persistent household demand for equities, while DB liability-matching sustains demand for bonds.
insights.quote: they make much safer investments into lower-return assets, such as bonds
insights.locator: Employees with DC pensions want to

insights.claim: Riskier DC portfolios expose households more to the business cycle, so their collective retirement assets can fall sharply in recessions.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A future equity drawdown would hit household retirement wealth harder now that DC assets dominate, potentially amplifying consumption pullbacks.
insights.quote: Households’ riskier investments in their DC pensions expose them more to the business cycle

insights.claim: During the Great Recession (2007 Q3 to 2009 Q1), private DC pension assets fell 30%, from $3.73 trillion to $2.60 trillion.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Benchmark for the scale of DC drawdowns in a severe downturn: applied to today's ~$12 trillion base, a similar shock would erase several trillion dollars.
insights.quote: The value of DC pension assets fell 30%, from $3.73 trillion to $2.60 trillion

insights.claim: Over the same Great Recession window, private DB pension assets actually grew 5%, from $2.46 trillion to $2.58 trillion, as safer allocations insulated them.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: DB portfolios behave defensively in equity crashes but, as 2021-2026 shows, are vulnerable to rising rates.
insights.quote: DB pension assets actually grew 5%, from $2.46 trillion to $2.58 trillion

insights.claim: DC pension assets offer far greater growth but are also far more volatile than DB assets; the tradeoff is higher returns for higher cyclical risk.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The shift toward DC raises both long-run household wealth and its sensitivity to market cycles.
insights.quote: But defined contribution pension assets are also far more volatile.

insights.claim: FRED series BOGZ1FL574090055Q (private DC pension total financial assets) and BOGZ1FL574090045Q (private DB pension total financial assets) track these pension asset levels from the Fed's Financial Accounts.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Quarterly trackable indicators for monitoring household equity exposure via retirement accounts.
